correction.summary: HIT: Iceland / Húnaþing vestra / Hvammstangi confirmed to within 0.42 km. The decisive readable evidence was the Icelandic orthography on the street blade ('Norður...braut', with ð), the hotel sign ending '-MSTANGI', and the clinic facade branded 'HEILBRIGÐISSTOFNUN VESTURLANDS' with Lyfja pharmacy — an HVE clinic on a wide north-facing bay. The Faroe Islands alternative was correctly excluded because the far shore is a long, low, even grassy tableland several km away rather than a steep terraced basalt sound wall, and the road suffix is '-braut', not '-vegur/-gøta'.

discriminators.title: Icelandic '-braut' street blades vs Faroese '-vegur/-gøta'
discriminators.body: In Iceland street-name blades use compounds ending in -braut, -gata, -vegur combined with cardinal prefixes like Norður-/Suður-, written with ð and á/ó. In the Faroes you would instead see -vegur/-gøta with Faroese vowel patterns (ø, ó, oy) and settlement names built on -vík/-oyri/-havn. The presence of ð alone never separates the two; the compound morphology does.

discriminators.title: Low flat-topped far shore across a wide bay = Iceland, not a Faroese sound
discriminators.body: In Iceland's north-west bays (Húnaflói/Miðfjörður) the opposite shore lies several kilometres away as a uniform, low, grass-covered tableland with no visible scree or hanging valleys. In the Faroes the far side of any sound rises steeply within a kilometre or two as terraced basalt cliffs with talus fans. Judge the distance and profile of the far skyline before committing.

discriminators.title: Read the Heilbrigðisstofnun acronym: HVE on a north-facing bay means Húnaþing vestra
discriminators.body: Icelandic clinics carry regional health-authority names that do not follow the coastline: HVE (Vesturlands) covers Húnaþing vestra even though Hvammstangi faces north onto Húnaflói. If a clinic on a north coast reads 'Norðurlands' (HSN) instead, you are further east at Blönduós, Skagaströnd or Sauðárkrókur. Do not translate 'Vesturlands' into a west-coast location.

discriminators.title: Planted spruce blocks on bare heath vs Norway's continuous forest
discriminators.body: In Iceland even coastal villages sit on treeless grass heath with geometric, sharply bounded plantations of spruce and low willow scrub. In mainland Norway at similar latitude natural boreal forest runs unbroken down to the shoreline and farmland is hedged and fenced. Rectangular dark conifer patches with abrupt straight edges are the Icelandic afforestation signature.

discriminators.title: Icelandic village core: white spire, rainbow crosswalk, blue-canopy fuel station
discriminators.body: Icelandic service villages cluster a small white concrete church with slender spire, a school with fenced sports pitch, a single blue/green-canopy fuel station and a rainbow-painted crosswalk within a few hundred metres. In Faroese villages you would instead see a tar-black timber church with white trim and turf or slate roof, and no franchise fuel canopy of that scale. Use this ensemble to confirm Iceland when signage is unreadable.
